concepts.title: Bile-acid feedback and bile-acid sequestrants
concepts.rationale: Adds the specific mechanism needed by retake questions that is absent from the existing chapter concepts.
concepts.summary: Cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the classical bile-acid synthesis pathway. Returning bile acids suppress expression of this enzyme, limiting their own synthesis through negative feedback. Most secreted bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and return to the liver in the enterohepatic circulation. Bile-acid sequestrants bind them in the intestinal lumen, increasing fecal loss and relieving feedback inhibition of synthesis. The liver consumes more cholesterol to replenish bile acids and increases uptake of circulating LDL cholesterol.
keyPoints: Bile acids suppress cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase.
Terminal-ileal reabsorption maintains the enterohepatic bile-salt pool.
Sequestrants prevent intestinal bile-acid reabsorption.
Increased conversion of hepatic cholesterol to bile acids helps lower plasma LDL.
clinicalLinks: Cholestyramine is a bile-acid sequestrant.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 18, pp. 224-227 (bile-acid synthesis, feedback, and sequestrants).

concepts.title: Late starvation shifts muscle away from ketones
concepts.rationale: Adds the specific mechanism needed by retake questions that is absent from the existing chapter concepts.
concepts.summary: Resting skeletal muscle relies increasingly on fatty acids as insulin falls during fasting. It can use both fatty acids and ketone bodies early in starvation, but after prolonged starvation it reduces ketone consumption and uses fatty acids as its principal fuel. This leaves more circulating ketones available to the brain. As brain glucose demand falls, the requirement for gluconeogenesis from muscle amino acids also decreases.
keyPoints: Resting muscle favors fatty acids during prolonged starvation.
Late reduction in muscle ketone use helps preserve ketones for the brain.
Brain ketone use reduces the need for muscle-protein breakdown.
These resting-starvation adaptations do not describe all exercise intensities.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 24, pp. 331-333 (resting skeletal muscle and brain in fasting).

concepts.title: Calcitriol increases intestinal absorption and renal calcium conservation
concepts.rationale: Adds the specific mechanism needed by retake questions that is absent from the existing chapter concepts.
concepts.summary: Calcitriol, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, is the active hormone derived from vitamin D. Its production involves 25-hydroxylation in the liver followed by 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney, with the latter stimulated by parathyroid hormone in response to low calcium. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption and helps increase renal tubular calcium reabsorption. It also works with parathyroid hormone to mobilize bone calcium when needed, while adequate vitamin D supports normal mineralization.
keyPoints: Calcitriol is active vitamin D, not a B-vitamin coenzyme.
The kidney performs the final activating hydroxylation.
Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium uptake and renal calcium reabsorption.
Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 28, pp. 385-388 (vitamin D activation and actions).

flags.reason: The keyed overview is broadly correct, but sugars need not pass through free glucose before glycolysis because fructose and other sugars can enter through glycolytic intermediates.

The keyed six ATP from two glycolytic NADH uses Lippincott 6e's historical three-ATP-per-NADH convention and assumes the malate–aspartate shuttle; modern accounting gives five with that shuttle, so the convention should be explicit.

The keyed hypoperfusion mechanism is appropriate, but its wording can imply that lactate formation itself generates protons even though the LDH reaction consumes H+ and the acidosis reflects the broader failure of oxidative energy metabolism.

The keyed GLUT2 description matches Lippincott 6e, but its general beta-cell sensing statement needs a species qualification because human beta cells predominantly express GLUT1 and much less GLUT2 than rodent beta cells.

The keyed propionyl-CoA answer describes a partial-pathway accounting convention, but "a comparable even-chain fatty acid" and the carbon endpoint are unspecified, so it does not establish a general complete-oxidation energy comparison.

ALT is the intended answer for greater liver specificity, but “more liver-enriched” is ambiguous because Lippincott states that the liver contains a larger absolute amount of AST (Chapter 19, pp. 251-252).
